claims.overstatement: None material. The claim correctly calls the heat-loss mechanism an inference (heat production was not measured), keeps the low dose and cocaine-naive sample as study conditions, and reports the clubs/hot-weather idea as untested speculation. Wording points: (1) 'skin blood flow was 49 against 70 in 100 of its maximum' is forearm cutaneous vascular conductance (laser-Doppler flux divided by mean arterial pressure, as % of the site maximum), as the magnitude says; because end-of-heating pressure was higher with cocaine (92 against 87 mm Hg), flow itself would differ somewhat less than conductance, so 'skin vascular conductance' or 'skin blood flow relative to blood pressure' is more exact. (2) The Figure 1 end values read about 37.79 against 37.55 C at about 38 min (gap about 0.23 C on the figure's own bracket), so '37.8 against 37.5' slightly widens the gap; 'about 37.8 against 37.55' would match the figure.
claims.note: All text numbers in the statement and magnitude match pp. 787-788. Editors' calculation recomputed: difference 0.31 C with paired t on 6 df; P = 0.01 gives t = 3.707, SE 0.084, 95% CI 0.105 to 0.515; P = 0.002 gives t = 5.208, SE 0.060, 95% CI 0.164 to 0.456; same as the claim (with P rounding, the first interval could run from about 0.09-0.13 to 0.49-0.54). 'Number contributing at 37.86 C not stated' is fair: the paper calls it the highest common oesophageal temperature without a count, and Figure 1 shows the lidocaine mean only about 37.55 C at the end of the plotted time. Text-figure inconsistency the claim inherits but does not need to fix: at the same temperature Figure 2 (p. 789) reads about 54 against 67% of maximum and about 0.86 against 1.07 mg/cm2 per min, and its legend gives P < 0.01, while the text gives 49 +/- 9 against 70 +/- 5% (P = 0.03) and 0.8 +/- 0.2 against 1.0 +/- 0.1 (P = 0.04). Sex split of the 7 participants not given.

anchors.locator: Methods > Participants, 1st paragraph; with the abstract (p. 785, Participants) and the last paragraph of the introduction (p. 786)
anchors.extracted: 7 healthy male and female volunteers aged 23 to 37 (abstract: cocaine-naive); normotensive, no history of cardiovascular disease, cocaine or other recreational drug use, no drugs with cardiovascular or autonomic effects; no smoking, alcohol or caffeine for at least 12 h. Introduction: a low, noneuphoric intranasal dose was chosen. Laboratory in Dallas, Texas.

anchors.locator: Methods > Experimental Protocol, 1st paragraph; Measurements, 1st paragraph (p. 786)
anchors.extracted: Supine, randomized, double-blind crossover: whole-body heating after intranasal cocaine hydrochloride 2 mg/kg (10% solution) or lidocaine hydrochloride 2 mg/kg (10% solution), lidocaine as a control for cocaine's local anaesthetic action; 2 days at the same time of day, 3-6 days apart; cocaine dose half the standard rhinolaryngological dose (study conditions). Heating by perfusing the tube-lined suit (whole body except head, arms, feet) with 46 C water; afterwards local skin heating to 42 C for 30 min to obtain maximal forearm conductance. Abstract calls lidocaine the placebo.

Before heat stress, oesophageal temperature 36.79 +/- 0.01 C with cocaine against 36.75 +/- 0.08 C with lidocaine (no effect); cocaine raised mean arterial pressure 93 +/- 3 against 85 +/- 3 mm Hg (P = 0.001) and heart rate 74 +/- 5 against 67 +/- 4 beats/min (P = 0.01); forearm cutaneous vascular conductance 9 +/- 2 against 7 +/- 2% of maximum (P = 0.09). Mean +/- SE.

anchors.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Figure 1 (bottom and top panels)
anchors.extracted: Cocaine augmented the progressive rise in oesophageal temperature during heating, P < 0.001 (Figure 1). Read from Figure 1 bottom by pixel position: end of plotted heating at about 38 min, cocaine about 37.79 C against lidocaine about 37.55 C (SE bars about 0.15 C each; bracket marks a gap of about 0.23 C). Skin temperature rose similarly under both conditions (Figure 1 top; Results 2nd paragraph), so the external heat load was comparable.

Oesophageal temperature threshold for onset of cutaneous vasodilation 37.37 +/- 0.09 C (cocaine) against 37.06 +/- 0.07 C (lidocaine), P = 0.01; for sweating 37.38 +/- 0.09 against 37.07 +/- 0.06 C, P = 0.002; slopes unchanged. Thresholds read from individual plots by an investigator blinded to participant and condition (p. 787). Editors' recomputation, paired t on 6 df: 0.31 C, 95% CI about 0.11 to 0.51 and 0.16 to 0.46 C.

At the highest common oesophageal temperature, 37.86 C, cutaneous vascular conductance 49 +/- 9 against 70 +/- 5% of maximum (P = 0.03) and forearm sweat rate 0.8 +/- 0.2 against 1.0 +/- 0.1 mg/cm2 per min (P = 0.04), lower with cocaine; number of participants contributing not stated. Figure 2 end points (about 37.87 C) read about 54 against 67% and about 0.86 against 1.07 mg/cm2 per min, legend P < 0.01.

anchors.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph (end); Figure 3 (p. 789); Methods > Statistical Analysis (p. 787)
anchors.extracted: Cocaine attenuated the rise in thermal discomfort although core temperature rose more; the difference became significant once oesophageal temperature exceeded 37.0 C and grew with temperature (P < 0.05). Analysis: oesophageal temperature compared at each perceived-heating rating from 5.0 to 7.5 on a 9-point scale (4.0 neutral to 8.0 unbearably hot) by paired t-tests, i.e. at each rating core temperature was higher with cocaine. No order effect found on any outcome.

anchors.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph; with Measurements (p. 786) and abstract Conclusions (p. 785)
anchors.extracted: Authors infer that because cocaine did not change core temperature without external heat, impaired heat dissipation rather than greater heat production was the dominant mechanism; no measure of heat production (metabolic rate) is listed among the measurements. Abstract calls impaired heat dissipation a major mechanism by which cocaine raises body temperature in humans. Threshold shift exceeded three times the 0.09 C test-retest variability of the sweating threshold reported elsewhere.

Authors stress the effect was seen with a very low, non-euphoric dose; larger doses producing intoxication, agitation and more movement would be expected to add heat production; impaired heat perception would blunt behavioural cooling responses.

Authors speculate (untested) that recreational doses in hot weather, crowded nightclubs or raves would greatly amplify the effect; study only in healthy cocaine-naive people, so results may not apply to long-term use (rodent studies show no tolerance or reverse tolerance).
